# Results — Study 215 (Big-Mac-PPP) on real tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Recipe: each July, read
the Economist Big Mac mis-valuation (% over/under-priced vs USD). Go **long the 3 most
under-valued** and **short the 3 most over-valued** currencies, entering August,
holding one year. The benchmark is an identical portfolio with **random rankings**
drawn i.i.d. each year, averaged over 20 seeds. As-of **2026-06-16**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n obs | Fingerprint |
|---|---|--:|---|
| Economist Big Mac index (hardcoded, July snapshots) + Yahoo Finance FX (annual) | 2000-2023 | 197 currency-year obs / **24 portfolio years** | `0d61618b411f` |

Currencies: EUR, GBP, JPY, CAD, AUD, CHF, SEK, NOK, MXN, BRL.
Forward return window: Aug(T) to Jul(T+1) to respect the July publication lag.

## The regression signal: does mis-valuation predict next-year FX?

The core PPP hypothesis: currencies with a higher Big Mac mis-valuation (more expensive
vs the US) should tend to *fall* against the dollar (negative slope expected).

| Statistic | Value |
|---|--:|
| n observations | 197 |
| OLS slope (% FX change per 1% mis-val) | **+0.03%** |
| t-stat on slope | **+1.35** |
| R-squared | **0.93%** |

The slope is **positive** (+0.03%), not negative as PPP predicts, and the t-stat of
**+1.35** is below the |t| >= 2 bar. The pooled regression finds no evidence that
Big Mac over-valuation predicts currency depreciation over the next year. The sign is
actually wrong — slightly over-valued currencies tend to appreciate in the next year,
consistent with the UIP / carry literature rather than PPP reversion.

## The honest test — PPP sort vs random-ranking control (gross, cost = 0)

| Arm | n years | Ann. mean | Ann. Sharpe | t-stat |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Big Mac PPP (long under-valued, short over-valued)** | 24 | **-2.00%** | **-0.29** | **-1.40** |
| Random-ranking control (20-seed avg) | 24 | -0.41% | — | — |
| PPP minus random | — | **-1.59%** | — | — |

- The PPP portfolio's gross annual return is **-2.00%**, t = **-1.40** — statistically
  indistinguishable from zero and in the wrong direction.
- It **does not beat the random control.** The random-ranking portfolio earns **-0.41%/yr**;
  the Big Mac sort *underperforms* by **-1.59%/yr**.
- Note: with only 24 annual observations the test has limited power even when |t| > 2
  would be required. The combination of wrong sign and small n is the critical failure.

## Could you trade it? — cost sweep (PPP portfolio, net)

Annual rebalance means very low turnover — at most one trade per currency pair per year.
Transaction costs are essentially irrelevant at annual frequency:

| Cost (per leg) | Net ann. mean | t-stat |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | -2.00% | -1.40 |
| 5 bps | -2.02% | -1.41 |
| 10 bps | -2.03% | -1.42 |
| 20 bps | -2.05% | -1.43 |
| 50 bps | -2.13% | -1.48 |

Costs are negligible at annual frequency — the strategy is not killed by costs, it
is killed by the absence of any signal. Even at 0 bps the gross is negative.

## Sub-period breakdown (gross)

| Period | n years | Ann. mean | t-stat |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2000-2007 | 8 | -2.14% | -1.55 |
| 2008-2015 | 8 | -1.21% | -0.39 |
| 2016-2023 | 8 | -2.65% | -0.92 |

No sub-period shows |t| > 2. The strategy is negative in all three sub-periods.
The 2000-2007 period (pre-GFC) was the one where PPP should have had the best chance
given the large USD over-valuation cycle — it still failed.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK (borderline NONE).** Gross t = -1.40, -2.00%/yr gross; slope of the
  cross-sectional regression is essentially zero (R2 = 0.93%) and *wrong-signed*. The
  Big Mac mis-valuation does not predict FX returns at a one-year horizon. PPP is a
  decades-long anchor, not a one-year trading signal.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Gross edge is already negative; the strategy's failure is
  not a cost problem (annual turnover is minimal) but a signal problem. There is no
  version of this that survives realistic implementation.
- **PPP claim — MIXED.** PPP holds very loosely in the long run (decades) but is
  empirically indistinguishable from zero at the one-year horizon, consistent with
  Rogoff's PPP puzzle and half-life estimates of 3-5 years.
